results.text: The thresholds used in this report can serve as approximate class boundaries. Each of the three poverty lines is the typical national poverty line of an income group: $3.00 a day for low-income economies, $4.20 for lower-middle-income economies, and $8.30 for upper-middle-income economies (refer to box 1.1). Households living on less than $3.00 a day are extremely poor by any standard. Those living on between $3.00 and $8.30 are above the extreme poverty line, but would count as poor in a middle-income economy and, for the most part, remain short of economic security. Those living on between $8.30 and $28.00 a day are above the poverty line of every developing economy and constitute a global middle class; and those above $28.00 a day exceed the prosperity standard this report uses to gauge shared prosperity (refer to chapter 2). These thresholds are proxies. Ongoing work indicates that

results.text: 22 POVERTY , PROSPERITY , AND PLANET REPORT 2026 in 2000 to a majority by 2026, and extreme poverty has all but disappeared. In today’s lower-middle-income economies, the group living on between $3.00 and $8.30 a day is now the largest, and the middle class, though growing, remains a minority. In low-income economies, the distribution has barely shifted. About half the population is still living on less than $3.00 a day, and the middle class is negligible. High-income economies, by contrast, are composed almost entirely of households living on more than $8.30 a day, and the majority are above the prosperity standard.
